$comment: Register of formal and test evidence for vultrino. See docs/dev/FORMAL.md. Only a CI run counts as evidence of record.

claims.statement: In the unit tests of src/formal_kernel.rs: the admission gate returns the written expected outcome for all 12 inputs (verdict Allow, Deny or Prompt; observe downgrade; approval required), so only Allow, or a Deny under an observe downgrade, without an approval requirement, yields a witness, and then only when the evaluation recorded what it judged; a direct permit's binding carries the judged credential, principal and params digest and a rule digest naming the witness kind (Allow or ObservedDeny); authorize refuses a payload whose recomputed binding differs from the permit's in any one of approval id, epoch, tenant, principal, credential, action, params digest or the approved flag, and refuses a payload that cannot be bound; the approved gate refuses a Deny and is valid exactly from the grant's issue time up to its expiry at the window edges.
claims.does_not_establish: Table and example tests over the kernel, not a proof. The gate inputs (the policy decision, whether observe mode downgrades a Deny, and the server's approval requirement) are computed outside the kernel and are trusted here. The rule digest is not recomputed from the payload; it is checked only where the permit is minted. Says nothing about which code builds the payload or about code that runs after authorize. Does not show that every plugin dispatch needs an authorized permit; only the structural refinement gate counts the two dispatch seams. The approved-permit path is exercised only through approved_gate here; the claim permit-binding-production exercises ExecutionPermit::approved with a real grant.

claims.statement: Kani bounded model checking (0.67.0, pure-kernel build without wasm plugins) shows, over every input of the admission gate (verdict, observe downgrade, approval required, and whether the evaluation could bind its params), that a witness exists exactly when the verdict is Allow, or Deny under an observe downgrade, approval is not required and the params were bound, with a kind naming which of the two; that a direct permit copies the judged credential, principal and params digest, the request id, tenant and action, and the kind's rule digest into its binding; that authorize succeeds exactly when the seven payload-determined fields equal the permit's and the payload does not claim approved execution for a direct permit, whatever the rule digest; that the approved gate refuses a Deny and is valid exactly on [issued, expires) for every i64 clock value; and that next_epoch never wraps. Each harness carries kani::cover statements that the CI vacuity gate requires to be satisfiable.
claims.does_not_establish: The detector runs each harness through formal/run-kani.sh, so it also fails when a harness reports no cover statement or an unsatisfiable one; that shows the harness is not vacuous, not that its covers are the right ones. Kani sees the kernel only: not the ActionPayload recomputation, not the policy engine that produces the Evaluation, not the approval module's grant derivation, and not ExecutionPermit::approved itself (only the pure approved_gate it calls). Each string field is drawn from two fixed values, so the authorize harness shows field-by-field equality is checked, not anything about string contents. Nothing under the wasm-plugins feature (Kani cannot build it). The gate inputs are trusted.

claims.statement: With the production policy engine (PolicyEngine::evaluate_for_admission and evaluate_readonly_for_admission, the only builders of the private Evaluation), the approval module's grant derivation and the production ActionPayload binding recomputation: a direct permit minted for one params value refuses a payload with other params (BindingMismatch), and so does an approved permit; changing the payload's credential alias, plugin, action, params, tenant, principal, approved flag, approval id or approval epoch after the mint is refused; an enforced Deny (a fail-closed engine with no policy) never yields a direct witness, with or without an approval requirement; an observe-only tenant's ordinary Deny yields only the ObservedDeny witness kind, which the permit keeps, and never for a kill switch or a RateLimit guard; a Prompt, or Allow with a server approval requirement, goes to approval; a Deny at resume refuses the approved permit, a resume evaluation of other params refuses it, and a Prompt at resume is satisfied by the grant.
claims.does_not_establish: The tests call the mint and authorize functions with production inputs; they do not run prepare_execution or resume_approved (the integration tests in tests/approval_token_integration.rs do, and the full-tier mutant permit-admit-approval-literal-false is detected by two of them). The kernel trusts its inputs: which policy rules matched, the tenant mode, and the server's approval requirement (credential flag, token, dual control, capability catalog). The binding's action is the canonical plugin.action the server resolved from the presented label, while the evaluation judged the label (ActionMatch); the kernel does not check that one resolves to the other. The rule digest is not recomputed from the payload. run_action unpacks the authorized payload and builds the plugin request after authorize; that code, and anything a plugin does with the payload, is not checked by the kernel. The params digest is over the serde_json bytes of the stored value, not over bytes an approver saw. authorize does not check the payload fields outside the binding: the credential record beyond its alias, the use token id, the evidence subject, the evidence action and whether Averin evidence is required; run_action acts on them after authorize. Covers only the two mint sites and their helpers by drift lock; other callers of the policy engine (for example list-time capability visibility) do not go through the kernel.

claims.statement: A recipe that requires an agent-reviewer term can never be satisfied even when fully signed, a recipe with an over-cap or overflowing count is unsatisfiable, and a senior sign-off on one aggregator key cannot fabricate several teammate slots, in the named unit tests.
claims.does_not_establish: Three example-based tests. They do not cover every recipe shape (see the Kani claims for bounded exhaustive coverage), the sign-off collection and deduplication code, or the match between these rules and govder's recipe evaluator.

claims.statement: Kani bounded model checking (0.67.0) over symbolic three-term recipes (4-iteration unwind), plus fixed empty, one-term and two-term malformed shapes in the malformed-recipe harness, shows: no recipe is satisfied with zero approvers, satisfaction never underfills a slot, malformed recipes are never satisfied, and the per-term cap prevents slot-need overflow.
claims.does_not_establish: Recipes with more than three terms or sign-off counts beyond the harness bounds. The detector runs each harness through formal/run-kani.sh, so it also fails when a harness reports no cover statement or an unsatisfiable one; that shows the harness is not vacuous, not that its covers are the right ones. Says nothing about sign-off collection, identity deduplication or separation of duties.

claims.statement: Kani bounded model checking (0.67.0) shows the greedy senior-first slot assignment in recipe_satisfied agrees with an exhaustive assignment search at the harness bound of 5, that satisfaction is monotone in the number of available approvers, and that class_fills_a_slot agrees with satisfaction.
claims.does_not_establish: The agreement is for availability and recipe counts within the harness bound of 5, not for all u32 values. The detector runs each harness through formal/run-kani.sh, so it also fails when a harness reports no cover statement or an unsatisfiable one; that shows the harness is not vacuous, not that its covers are the right ones. The exhaustive reference is written in the same harness module, so a shared misreading of the intended rule would not be caught.

claims.statement: The outbound-request address classifier blocks the first and last address of every IANA special-purpose registry row marked not globally reachable, as transcribed by hand into the test (plus 2001::/23 and multicast), and keeps the tested neighbouring addresses reachable, and it decodes IPv4 carried in IPv4-mapped, NAT64 and 6to4 IPv6 addresses before classifying, in the named unit tests.
claims.does_not_establish: Table-driven tests over listed addresses, not an exhaustive check of the address space. The registry rows were transcribed by hand from IANA tables retrieved on one date. The drift lock covers the functions and the IPV4_BLOCKED and IPV6_BLOCKED tables, so an edited row needs a deliberate relock; the tests still check only the listed addresses of each row. DNS rebinding, redirects and proxies are separate controls this claim does not cover.

claims.statement: A periodic policy refresh that has already listed stored policies cannot overwrite a newer admin reload that carries a kill policy: both load paths take one in-process async load lock across ticket, vault re-read, list and apply (with a ticket compare as a second guard), in a scripted interleaving test that starts an admin write and reload inside the refresh window, waits 150 ms, and checks the admin reload has not finished and the kill policy survives. A second scripted interleaving (the refresh takes its ticket first, a local admin reload waits, then another process writes a kill policy to the same vault) checks that the refresh re-reads the vault and the kill policy becomes live.
claims.does_not_establish: Two scripted interleavings, not a model of all schedules. The wait check relies on a 150 ms sleep: on a very slow machine a mutant could survive, but the unmutated code cannot fail it, because the admin reload is blocked on the lock. The lock is per process: another process's write becomes visible only on the next refresh tick, so cross-process visibility is bounded-staleness, not instant. Cross-process visibility in the second test is the same bounded staleness: the test writes before the refresh re-read, it does not show the write is seen if it lands after. Removing only the ticket compare (the second guard) is not detected by this test. Does not cover other policy load paths that call load_policies directly (construction and tests) or a lost write in storage itself.

claims.statement: The fixed-window rate limiter transition function reproduces, byte for byte, the committed trace fixture formal/vectors/rate_limiter_traces.json (cold start, sub-window lag, exact whole-window lag, two-window lag), and an invalid limiter (max 0 or window 0) denies without creating state.
claims.does_not_establish: The fixture is generated by the same function it checks, so it pins current behaviour against silent change; it is not an independent specification. A govder consumer of the same fixture exists only on an unmerged govder branch, so no cross-repo agreement is established. The Instant-based adapter that feeds window_elapsed is not covered.

claims.statement: A credential minted or refreshed during an action (OAuth2 refresh, Google service-account mint) is added to the scrub set, so an upstream that reflects it in headers or body does not leak it to the agent on the buffered and streamed paths; a minted secret shorter than the redaction floor causes the whole response to be withheld on both paths, in the named integration tests.
claims.does_not_establish: Mock plugins reflecting fixed token shapes; other reflection encodings and other credential types are not tested here. The scrub-set extension is the drift-locked helper egress::scrub_set_with_minted; its two call sites in VultrinoServer::run_action and run_action_streaming (src/server/mod.rs) are not drift-locked, and the integration tests are their only guard. A plugin error path that echoes a minted secret is a documented residual in docs/dev/LIMITATIONS.md.

claims.statement: The set of spellings the response scrub removes for a credential's secret includes, for each secret of at least 5 bytes: the raw value, its percent-encodings (full, lowercase hex, form-url plus, and the JS encodeURIComponent, Python quote, Go url.PathEscape and RFC 3986 pchar safe sets), its JSON-escaped forms (plain, slash-escaped, ensure_ascii, HTML-safe, and two further nested levels of the plain and slash-escaped spelling), and its whole-value base64 (standard and URL alphabet, padded and unpadded) and hex (both cases) spellings, and, for a value of at least 14 bytes, the base64 (standard and URL alphabet, unpadded) of the whole 3-byte groups of the value at each of its three alignments, so the base64 of a longer string such as Bearer <token> is scrubbed apart from at most 2 bytes at each end. The decoded Basic user:password and OAuth2 client_id:client_secret composites are secret material, so every one of those spellings of the composite is also removed. The buffered redaction, the incremental stream scrubber and the final confine_response postcondition use the one set; the named unit tests reflect each spelling through the buffered path, and the base64 and hex spellings through the stream scrubber as well; the base64 core test drives the buffered and streamed paths only, and confine_response is covered by sharing the one form set.
claims.does_not_establish: Whole-value spellings and whole-group base64 cores only: a hash of the secret, an encoding other than base64 of a longer string that contains it, a base64 core shorter than 16 characters (a value under 14 bytes), a value split across separate SSE events or lines, a spelling in a dialect not listed, and a reflection in a header NAME are not covered, and the scrub stays byte-exact defense in depth against an upstream that reflects by accident, not against one that encodes on purpose. The unit tests use one value with the characters that make the spellings differ; the end-to-end reflection through the running binary is the govder claim e2e-credential-canary-scan. Secrets shorter than 5 bytes are handled by withholding the response, not by this set.

claims.statement: Verified approver decisions use a dedicated approval key only: with the key unset, equal to the shared govder key, or equal after trimming whitespace, verified approvals are disabled unless the explicit shared-key escape is set, in the named unit tests.
claims.does_not_establish: The unit tests cover the key-selection function. They pad only the shared key; the dedicated key is trimmed at load by approval_assertion_secret_from_env, which is not drift-locked and not exercised here. The 403 on the decision route (api_decide_approval) has route-level tests in tests/web_smoke.rs that run in the rust job, but they are not registered, not run by this detector and not drift-locked. Key strength, key distribution and whether the broker signs with the dedicated key are operational matters.

claims.statement: formal/check-refinement.py checks source shape only: the Rust ExecutionBinding field list equals the Lean RequestBinding field list, and a fixed list of seams, strings and Lean theorem names are still present in the source. Register this as a structural gate, not a refinement proof.
claims.does_not_establish: Semantic refinement of Rust by the Lean model. It greps for strings and counts call sites; code can keep every string and still behave differently. The drift lock covers src/formal_kernel.rs only, while the script reads many other files.

claims.statement: Model-level result: in the hand-written Lean model of the execution boundary, every reachable state records only properly authorized executions and never consumes the same approval binding twice (Approval.reachable_execution_is_proper and reachable_approval_consumption_is_one_shot), checked with lake build --wfail.
claims.does_not_establish: A property of the Lean model, not of the Rust code: the model is hand-written and not extracted from Rust, and the link is the structural refinement gate only. The detector runs lake build, not the independent nanoda check that CI also runs. ExecutionSafety.lean, Model.lean and Types.lean are drift-locked. The one-shot theorem is stated over the consumed-binding list: it means at most one execution per approval binding only together with State.afterExecute recording every approved binding (a model change that stopped recording would keep the theorem true). reachable_execution_is_proper holds by construction (an Execution carries its permit, and proper_of_permit makes every Execution proper), so it shows nothing about the transition system. The one-shot theorem is per RequestBinding, which includes the execution epoch, and the Rust code mints a fresh epoch per claim, so this is not at most one execution per approval id.

claims.statement: vultrino's recipe satisfaction function agrees with the committed shared vector file src/approval/testdata/recipe_vectors.json (byte-identical to govder internal/oversight/testdata/recipe_vectors.json; both sides pin its sha256), including the rows that are unrepresentable and the rows whose agent-reviewer terms must be unsatisfiable.
claims.does_not_establish: Agreement only on the committed vectors and on the sweep domain they were generated over. The govder half runs only in govder CI, not here: this claim shows vultrino matches the file, and the pinned hash shows the file did not change, not that govder currently matches it. Two implementations can agree and both be wrong (the exhaustive claims check correctness against an independent oracle over a bounded domain). Says nothing about sign-off collection or identity handling.

claims.statement: recipe_satisfied agrees with an independent maximum-matching oracle at every point of three committed sweeps (human axis, agent-reviewer simplex, cap cliff), senior-first greedy equals the oracle over the sweep domain, and the oracle itself is shown to discriminate a wrong implementation.
claims.does_not_establish: Only the sweep domains named in the vector file (small need and availability bounds plus the cap cliff). Not a proof for all counts. The oracle is a second hand-written implementation in the same test module, not an extracted specification. Sweeps check satisfaction, not sign-off collection.

claims.statement: At the real per-term cap of 64, the senior-first greedy rule in recipe_satisfied agrees with an independent split-search oracle on all 9,628,905 points of need (senior, teammate) with ns+nt <= 64 against availability 0..=65 plus u32::MAX for each class (no agent-reviewer slots), and the split-search oracle agrees with the unit matching oracle on the 4,500-point cube (need sum at most 8, availability 0..=9 per class).
claims.does_not_establish: Only the enumerated domain: a recipe with one senior term and one teammate term, no agent-reviewer slots (those are unsatisfiable by a fixed guard, covered by the vector claim). Availability above 65 is argued, not enumerated, to behave like 65; that argument and the finiteness of the recipe axis rest on recipe_well_formed's caps, which the Kani and vector claims cover, so this claim is a composition inside one plane. Recipes with several alternative terms are not enumerated here. The oracles are test-local code.

claims.statement: The approval decision transition accepts or rejects every one of 720 enumerated states (status, target, executed flag, veto window, approver kind, ttl expiry, identity shape) exactly as an independently written legality oracle says, including the guard order (a blank identity is refused before the ttl check).
claims.does_not_establish: Only the 720 enumerated states, with three identity shapes and two approver kinds; no recipe-gated or multi-approver sequences (the property claim samples those). The oracle is hand-written in the test file. Says nothing about persistence, concurrency or the API layer that calls the transition. The detector also runs an_unnamed_principal_fills_no_slot, but approval_rule_satisfied and the bare-identity drop are not drift-locked and no mutant targets them, so that test is not part of this claim.

claims.statement: The closed wire and state decisions are enumerated over listed inputs: of ten listed risk-tier strings only Low, Medium and High (after trimming) do not force deny-on-any-deny (Extreme, blank, lower-case, upper-case and unknown spellings force it), of six listed approver-class strings only the three class names (after trimming) parse, the recipe decision-mode JSON decodes every listed shape to deny-on-any-deny except the one majority spelling, and the execution-state classifier matches its oracle over all 80 combinations of status, executed, failed and credential check.
claims.does_not_establish: Listed spellings only (ten risk-tier strings, six class strings, nine JSON shapes), not every possible string. The execution-state oracle is a restatement of the same rules in test code. Does not show the callers use these functions on every path, nor the Lean model of execution.

claims.statement: For 20,000 generated sequences of approve and deny decisions (numeric and recipe gated, several identity shapes including blank and aggregator-prefixed), every state produced by the real transition passes the vault shape check, survives a serde round trip unchanged, and passes the shape check again after decoding.
claims.does_not_establish: Random sampling with a fixed case count, not an exhaustive or symbolic check; decision sequences are at most 6 long with at most 3 required approvals. It checks that transition output satisfies validate_vault_shape, so a defect that both functions share would pass. Does not cover load-time handling of a tampered vault file beyond the shape check, nor state reached by paths other than approve and deny.

claims.statement: The config-time check on llm.provider_base rejects the link-local and cloud-metadata range in every listed spelling (dotted, decimal and hex IPv4, IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64, 6to4, fe80::/10, the AWS IPv6 metadata address) and accepts the listed neighbouring addresses, through is_link_local_or_metadata_ip.
claims.does_not_establish: One example-based test over listed spellings, not the address space. This is a config-time defence in depth; the execute-time classifier is covered by ssrf-special-purpose. Hostnames that resolve to metadata addresses (DNS), redirects and a provider_base changed after validation are not covered. Loopback and RFC1918 provider bases are deliberately allowed.

claims.statement: On the listed addresses, the internal_http destination classifier admits the loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT and unique-local examples, refuses the link-local, documentation, multicast, broadcast, NAT64 and 6to4 examples and the Alibaba (100.100.100.200) and AWS IPv6 (fd00:ec2::254) metadata endpoints, and each admitted example is one the public-only http guard refuses.
claims.does_not_establish: Listed addresses only, not an exhaustive check of the address space. Says nothing about hostname resolution, redirects or connect-time rebinding for internal_http, nor the allowlist configured per capability. Other cloud metadata endpoints not on the list are not tested.

claims.statement: Model-level result (Lean 4, hand-written model, not extracted from Rust): a broker-verified approval identity has exactly the tenant, approval id, outcome, subject, class, method, path, query, host and body digest that its evidence bound (verified_broker_identity_is_exact), evidence cannot validate any changed tuple (changed_binding_rejected), and a bare aggregator-key claim carries no independent-authentication witness while a verified broker claim is named.
claims.does_not_establish: These theorems unfold the definitions they are about (validFor requires binding equality, and independentlyAuthenticated is defined per evidence kind), so they pin those definitions against change rather than derive new facts. Nothing about the MAC primitive, the HTTP parser or the TTL clock source, which are trusted-computing-base assumptions. The one-positive-slot-per-key guard for aggregator claims is not modelled here, only that such claims are not independent. A property of the Lean model of the decision, not of the Rust code: the model is hand-written, and the only link to the shipped code is the structural refinement gate and the tests. The detector runs lake build for this module, not the independent nanoda check that CI also runs. The mutant is a definition change under which the theorem is false (a counterexample was type-checked against the mutated model), not only a broken proof script.
